decisions.quote:
While the percentage of journals that do not state their
position on this matter or implicitly discourage replications is similar to that in Yeung’s (2017) study

of neuroscience journals, the percentage of journals that explicitly accept replications is larger in

neuroscience (6%) and psychology journals (4%; Martin and Clarke 2017). It is possible that translation

and interpreting journals receive such low numbers of replicated studies for review, that explicit
statements about replications are not felt to be necessary.
decisions.reason: The shipped outcome quote comes from Section 4.3 (Results), which merely reports the raw counts for translation and interpreting journals without comparing them to Yeung (2017). In Section 5.5 (Discussion), the author explicitly compares Study 3's results to Yeung (2017), stating that the percentages of journals that do not state a position on replication (82.4% vs. 84.7%) or implicitly discourage replications (9.9% overall / 11.4% active vs. 8.6%) are similar to Yeung (2017), whereas the percentage of journals that explicitly accept replications is larger in neuroscience (6% vs. 0.8%). Under the codebook rules (Rule 2 and mixed), because no overall replication verdict is stated and the explicit comparison marks some findings as similar and another as differing, the outcome is 'mixed'.

corrected_value.authors: Makel, Matthew C., Jonathan A. Plucker, and Boyd Hegarty.
corrected_value.title: Replications in Psychology Research

decisions.quote: To complement the survey results, a bibliometric approach was used to identify replications in the TIS literature by carrying out a conceptual replication of Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty’s (2012) study on replication in psychology research. While the original study was conducted by analyzing only 100 journals with the highest 5-year impact factor in the field of psychology, in the present study, the bibliometric analysis was carried out using BITRA (Franco Aixelá 2001–2019).
decisions.location: Section 3.2 Study 2: Bibliometric analysis of replications in BITRA, lines 836-843 (with comparisons in Section 5.2, lines 2368-2425)
decisions.reason: Omitted target in the shipped dataset. Study 2 explicitly conducts a conceptual replication of Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty (2012) using the BITRA database and directly compares its bibliometric findings against Makel et al. (2012) in Section 5.2. Those comparisons are mixed: the author notes that the overall published replication rate is higher in psychology (1.07% vs. 0.06% in BITRA) and that self-replications make up 52.9% of replications in Makel et al. (2012) versus 30.4% in BITRA (where replications of others' studies predominate at 65.2%), while the low proportion of exact replications is described as not very different from Makel et al. (8.7% in BITRA vs. 14% in psychology).
